analysis.one_liner: Raises the tax-free estate exemption to $5 million and keeps the estate tax on larger fortunes permanently.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and no committee action, and expired when the Congress ended without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The estate tax law then in effect was set to repeal the tax entirely for one year in 2010 and then snap back in 2011 to its old form: a $1 million exemption with a 55% rate above that. This bill would have ended that schedule. Instead, it would have set a permanent exemption of $5 million, adjusted for inflation, and kept the tax above that amount at the pre-2001 top rate of 55%. Estates under $5 million would never owe the tax; the largest fortunes would keep paying it.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth up to $5 million would owe no estate tax — a group that includes many family-owned businesses and farms, and that would have been spared the 2011 snap-back to a $1 million exemption. The Treasury and, indirectly, other taxpayers would benefit from keeping a permanent tax on the very largest estates, which the bill would have set at the old 55% top rate above the $5 million line.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the estate and gift tax exemption at $5 million, up from $2 million in 2007 and $3.5 million under the law scheduled for 2009, so no estate under that amount owes the tax [S2][S3].
Indexes the $5 million exemption to inflation after 2010, so the protection grows over time instead of shrinking in real value [S2][S3].

Repeals the one-year full repeal of the estate tax in 2010 and the scheduled return of the old $1 million exemption and pre-2001 rates in 2011, replacing both with a single permanent rule — ending a decade of uncertainty for families planning inheritances [S2][S3].
Keeps a tax on the largest fortunes: estates above $5 million would pay the pre-2001 top rate, which CRS describes as restoring the previous estate tax structure [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury loses revenue on estates between the old exemption levels and $5 million, a cost ultimately shared by other taxpayers. Estates above $5 million would pay more than under the 2009 law — the pre-2001 top rate rather than the reduced 45% then in effect — and wealthy families would keep paying for avoidance planning.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury and estates above $5 million

drawbacks.text: Raising the exemption to $5 million forgives tax on a large band of wealth that was taxable under both the 2007 law ($2 million) and the scheduled 2009 law ($3.5 million), reducing federal revenue [S2][S3].

Restoring the pre-2001 rate structure means a 55% top rate on estates above $5 million — among the highest rates in the tax code — which critics of the old estate tax argued drove costly avoidance planning and was hard on heirs facing large estates [S2].

Because the bill repealed the 2001 law's estate tax provisions as if never enacted, it also undid the rate reductions that had been in effect since 2001, so some very large estates would face a steeper bill than the one then current [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered something rare in the estate tax fight: permanence. Families would have known the rules for good, and the tax would have stayed on the books for the largest fortunes at a steep rate, while exempting everything under $5 million. The trade-off is real on both sides — a much larger untaxed band gives up revenue that other taxpayers implicitly cover, and the restored 55% top rate is punishing to heirs of estates just over the line. Whether that balance is good depends heavily on how much one values a progressive tax on very large inheritances versus the revenue given up below $5 million.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, sat there with no cosponsors and no action, and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Capuano, a Massachusetts Democrat, introduced the bill on September 5, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S2][S5].
No cosponsors signed on, and the committee never took it up [S4][S5].
The bill expired on January 3, 2009, with no vote ever scheduled in the House [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax followed the schedule Congress had already written: it stayed at reduced rates through 2009, disappeared entirely for 2010, and returned in 2011. Heirs to the very largest fortunes came out ahead relative to what this bill would have done, since they kept the one-year tax-free window it would have repealed, and no family got the permanent $5 million exemption it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Heirs of the very largest estates

for.name: Rep. Michael Capuano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set a permanent $5 million estate tax exemption and keep the tax on larger estates; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only supporter was its single Democratic sponsor, and no one is recorded as opposing it either.

industries.industry: Heirs to multimillion-dollar estates and their families
industries.note: Estates worth $2 million to $5 million would have paid nothing instead of the estate tax, and estates up to $5 million would have been spared the scheduled 2011 snap-back to a $1 million exemption. Estates above $5 million would have paid the restored pre-2001 top rate of 55%, more than the 45% rate then in effect. The interest of large estates runs against ordinary taxpayers to the extent that forgiving the tax below $5 million shifts costs to the Treasury.

A single permanent rule with a $5 million exemption would have reduced the need for the elaborate planning that the 2010 repeal-then-snap-back schedule made lucrative. Simpler, more predictable rules mean less billable avoidance work.
